Chapter 3: Cybersecurity, Ethics and 
Emerging Technologies
These notes are based on Module 3 of your syllabus and cover:
● Information Security and Security Threats
● Cyber-attacks and Security Controls
● Privacy and Ethical Issues in Information Systems
● AI Ethics and Responsible AI
● Cybersecurity Incidents and Digital Governance
3.1 Information Security and Security 
Threats
1. Meaning of Information Security
Information Security means protecting information and information systems from:
● Unauthorized access
● Unauthorized use
● Unauthorized modification
● Disclosure of confidential information
● Destruction or loss of information
● Disruption of information systems 
In simple words:
Information security means ensuring that the right information is available to 
the right people, at the right time, and is protected from unauthorized people 
and harmful activities.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
Consider a college's student database. 
It contains:
● Student names
● Marks
● Attendance
● Phone numbers
● Fee information
The database should be protected so that:
● Only authorized people can access it.
● Nobody can secretly change marks.
● The information is not deleted accidentally.
● Sensitive information is not leaked.
All these protections together are part of Information Security.
2. CIA Triad
The three fundamental goals of information security are:
1. Confidentiality
2. Integrity
3. Availability
Together, they are called the CIA Triad.
CIA here does not refer to the intelligence agency. It stands for 
Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability.
2.1 Confidentiality
Confidentiality means protecting information from unauthorized access or disclosure. 
Only authorized people should be able to see sensitive information.

rects.text: Only authorized people should be able to see sensitive information.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
A student's examination marks should be accessible to:
● The student
● Authorized teachers
● The examination department
An unknown person should not be able to access or download everyone's marks.
Methods used to maintain confidentiality
● Passwords
● Encryption
● Authentication
● Access control
● Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)
Simple Example
Your WhatsApp messages should only be visible to you and the intended recipient. If a stranger 
reads them without permission, confidentiality has been violated.
2.2 Integrity
Integrity means ensuring that information remains:
● Accurate
● Complete
● Correct
● Unchanged unless modified by an authorized person
Example
Suppose a student originally scores 75 marks.
If someone illegally changes the marks from 75 to 95, the integrity of the data has been 
compromised.
Similarly, if a bank account balance is ₹10,000 and someone changes it to ₹1,00,000 without 
authorization, this is an integrity violation.
Methods used to maintain integrity

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Access controls
● Digital signatures
● Hashing
● Audit trails
● Backups
2.3 Availability
Availability means ensuring that information and systems are accessible when authorized
users need them.
Example
During online examination registration, thousands of students may access the university 
website.
If the website crashes and students cannot register, the availability of the system has been 
affected.
Methods used to maintain availability
● Regular system maintenance
● Data backups
● Redundant servers
● Disaster recovery systems
● Protection against Denial-of-Service attacks
2.4 Understanding the CIA Triad Through One Example
Imagine an online banking system:
Security Goal Meaning Example
Confidentiality Only authorized people can see 
information
Only the account holder can view their 
bank balance
Integrity Information remains correct Nobody can illegally change the 
account balance

3. Security Threat
A security threat is any potential danger that can harm an information system or its data. 
A threat may come from:
● Hackers
● Malicious software
● Employees
● Human mistakes
● System failures
● Natural disasters
Example
A hacker attempting to steal customer passwords is a security threat.
However, even an employee accidentally deleting an important database can become a threat 
to information security.
4. Types of Security Threats
4.1 Malware
Malware stands for Malicious Software.
It is software designed to harm, disrupt, steal information from, or gain unauthorized access to a 
computer system.
Common types include:
● Virus
● Worm
● Trojan Horse
● Ransomware

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Spyware
Virus
A computer virus attaches itself to a file or program and can spread when that file is executed.
Example
A person downloads an infected file. When they open it, the virus infects other files on the 
computer.
Worm
A worm is malware that can automatically spread from one computer to another, usually 
through networks.
Unlike many viruses, a worm does not necessarily require a user to open an infected file to 
spread.
Trojan Horse
A Trojan Horse appears to be legitimate software but secretly performs harmful activities.
Example
A user downloads a fake game that appears normal. In the background, it steals passwords 
from the computer.
Ransomware
Ransomware is malware that locks or encrypts a victim's data and demands money for 
restoring access.
Example
A company opens an infected email attachment. Its important files become inaccessible, and 
the attackers demand payment to restore them.

Spyware
Spyware secretly collects information about a user. 
It may collect:
● Browsing activity
● Passwords
● Personal information
● Other sensitive data
4.2 Phishing
Phishing is a cyber-attack in which attackers pretend to be a trusted person or organization to 
trick users into revealing sensitive information.
The attacker may send:
● Fake emails
● Fake messages
● Fake websites
Example
You receive an email saying:
"Your bank account will be blocked. Click here immediately to verify your account."
The link takes you to a fake website that looks like the real bank website. When you enter your 
username and password, the attacker steals them.
This is phishing.
4.3 Social Engineering
Social engineering means manipulating people into revealing confidential information or 
performing actions that help an attacker.
Instead of directly attacking a computer, the attacker targets human behaviour.

Example
An attacker calls an employee and says:
"Hello, I am from the IT department. We need your password to fix a technical 
problem."
If the employee believes the attacker and provides the password, the attack succeeds.
Important idea:
In many cyber-attacks, the weakest point is not the computer. It is the human being 
using the computer.
4.4 Password Attacks
Attackers may try to gain access by stealing, guessing or cracking passwords.
Example
Using a weak password such as:
Sbis1234
makes it easier for an attacker to guess compared with a strong and unique password.
4.5 Denial-of-Service (DoS) Attack
A Denial-of-Service attack attempts to make a system or website unavailable to legitimate 
users.
The attacker overwhelms the system with excessive requests or traffic.
Example
Imagine a website can normally handle 10,000 visitors.
An attacker sends millions of unnecessary requests. The server becomes overloaded, and 
genuine users cannot access the website.
This affects Availability.

4.6 Insider Threat
An insider threat comes from someone inside an organization who has legitimate access to 
information or systems.
This may be:
● An employee
● A former employee
● A contractor
● Another authorized user
The threat may be intentional or accidental.
Example 1: Intentional
An employee deliberately copies customer data and sells it.
Example 2: Accidental
An employee accidentally sends confidential company information to the wrong person.
5. Cyber-Attacks
A cyber-attack is an intentional attempt to:
● Access a system without authorization
● Steal information
● Damage data
● Disrupt services
● Gain financial or other benefits
A simple attack process can be understood as:
Find a weakness → Exploit the weakness → Gain access → Perform harmful 
activity
Example

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
A company uses weak passwords.
An attacker discovers this weakness, gains access to an employee's account and then steals 
confidential customer information.
6. Security Controls
Security controls are measures used to prevent, detect or reduce security risks. 
They help organizations protect their:
● Data
● Computers
● Networks
● Applications
● Users
Security controls can be broadly understood as:
1. Preventive controls
2. Detective controls
3. Corrective controls
6.1 Preventive Controls
Preventive controls try to stop an attack before it happens.
Examples
● Strong passwords
● Firewalls
● Multi-Factor Authentication
● Access control
● Employee security training
● Encryption
Example
A website requires both:

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Password
● OTP on the user's phone
This makes unauthorized access more difficult. Therefore, Multi-Factor Authentication acts as a
preventive control.
6.2 Detective Controls
Detective controls help an organization identify that a security incident has happened or is 
happening.
Examples
● Security monitoring
● Intrusion detection systems
● Audit logs
● Suspicious login alerts
Example
Suppose you normally log into your account from India, but suddenly someone attempts to log 
in from another country.
The system sends you an alert.
This is a detective control because it detects suspicious activity.
6.3 Corrective Controls
Corrective controls help an organization recover after a security incident.
Examples
● Data backups
● Disaster recovery
● System restoration
● Incident response procedures
Example

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
A ransomware attack encrypts a company's files.
The company removes the malware and restores its files from a secure backup. 
This is a corrective control.
6.4 Security Controls at Different Levels
Security is not only about installing antivirus software. Organizations use different types of 
controls.
Technical Controls 
These use technology. 
Examples:
● Firewalls
● Encryption
● Antivirus software
● Multi-Factor Authentication
Administrative Controls
These involve rules, policies and procedures. 
Examples:
● Security policies
● Employee training
● Password policies
● Access management procedures
Physical Controls
These protect physical resources. 
Examples:
● Security guards
● CCTV cameras
● Locked server rooms
● Biometric access

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
7. Privacy in Information Systems
Privacy refers to an individual's right to control how their personal information is collected, used, 
stored and shared.
Personal information may include:
● Name
● Phone number
● Email address
● Location
● Financial information
● Browsing behaviour
Example
Suppose a mobile application collects a user's location even when location data is unnecessary 
for its service.
This can create a privacy concern.
8. Privacy Issues in Information Systems
Common privacy issues include:
● Collection of excessive personal data
● Data sharing without permission
● Unauthorized access to personal information
● Data breaches
● Excessive tracking of users
● Using personal data for purposes not clearly explained
Example
A shopping website collects your name and address to deliver a product. That may be 
necessary.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
However, if the website secretly shares your information with many unrelated organizations, this 
creates a privacy issue.
9. Ethical Issues in Information Systems
Ethics refers to principles that help us decide what is right and wrong.
In Information Systems, an action may be technically possible but still be ethically wrong.
Example
A company may have the technical ability to track every website visited by its employees. 
But the question is:
Should the company track everything?
This is an ethical question.
Common Ethical Issues
1. Privacy
Is personal information being collected and used fairly?
2. Accuracy
Is the information correct?
3. Ownership
Who owns digital information?
4. Access
Who should be allowed to access information?

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
Suppose a company collects customer data for delivering products.
Later, it decides to use that data for another completely unrelated purpose without informing 
customers.
Even if the company can technically do this, the action may raise serious ethical concerns.
10. Difference Between Privacy and 
Security
These two concepts are closely related but different.
Security
Security focuses on protecting information from unauthorized access, loss or damage.
Privacy
Privacy focuses on how personal information is collected, used and shared.
Example
A company may have very strong security, but still have poor privacy practices.
Suppose a company securely stores customer data but collects much more personal 
information than necessary.
● The security may be strong.
● The privacy practice may still be questionable.
3.2 AI Ethics and Responsible AI
11. Meaning of AI Ethics

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
AI Ethics refers to the principles and values that guide the responsible development and use of 
Artificial Intelligence.
AI systems can affect important decisions involving:
● Education
● Employment
● Banking
● Healthcare
● Business
● Government services
Therefore, AI systems should not simply be judged by the question:
"Does the AI work?"
We should also ask:
"Does the AI work fairly, safely and responsibly?"
12. Major AI Ethics Issues
12.1 Bias and Fairness
Bias occurs when an AI system produces unfair or systematically unequal outcomes.
AI systems learn from data. If the data contains unfair patterns, the AI may reproduce those 
patterns.
Example
Suppose an AI system is trained using historical hiring data that mostly contains successful 
candidates from one particular group.
The AI may learn patterns that unfairly disadvantage other qualified candidates. 
Therefore:
Unfair data can lead to unfair AI decisions.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
12.2 Transparency
Transparency means that the functioning and decisions of an AI system should be 
understandable to an appropriate extent.
Example
Suppose a bank uses AI to reject a loan application. 
The applicant asks:
"Why was my loan rejected?"
If nobody can explain the decision, there is a lack of transparency.
12.3 Accountability
Accountability means that individuals or organizations should be responsible for the outcomes 
of AI systems.
Example
A company uses an AI system to make an incorrect decision that seriously harms a customer. 
The company should not simply say:
"The AI made the decision, so nobody is responsible."
Humans and organizations remain responsible for how AI systems are designed, deployed and 
monitored.
12.4 Privacy
AI systems may require large amounts of data. 
Organizations must carefully consider:
● What data is being collected?
● Why is it needed?
● Who can access it?

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● How long will it be stored?
● Is personal information properly protected?
12.5 Safety and Reliability
AI systems should work reliably and should be properly tested before being used for important 
decisions.
Example
If an AI system provides incorrect information in a casual entertainment application, the impact 
may be small.
However, if an AI system makes an incorrect decision in a high-impact environment, the 
consequences can be much more serious.
Therefore, the required level of testing and human oversight depends on how important the AI 
system's decisions are.
13. Responsible AI
Responsible AI means designing, developing and using AI in a manner that is:
● Fair
● Safe
● Transparent
● Accountable
● Privacy-conscious
● Reliable 
In simple words:
Responsible AI means using AI in a way that benefits people while reducing 
unfairness, harm and unnecessary risks.
14. Principles of Responsible AI

rects.text: consequences can be much more serious.

slides.text:
SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
1. Fairness
AI should avoid unjust discrimination.
2. Transparency
Important AI decisions should be understandable and appropriately explainable.
3. Accountability
Humans and organizations should remain responsible for AI systems.
4. Privacy
Personal data should be handled responsibly.
5. Safety
AI systems should be tested and monitored.
6. Human Oversight
Humans should remain involved where AI decisions have significant consequences.
15. Simple Example of Responsible AI
Suppose a company uses AI to screen job applications. 
A responsible approach would include:
1. Checking whether the training data contains unfair patterns.
2. Testing the system for biased outcomes.
3. Reviewing how the AI makes recommendations.
4. Keeping humans involved in important decisions.
5. Protecting applicants' personal data.
6. Regularly monitoring the system after deployment.
This demonstrates the idea of Responsible AI.

3.3 Case Studies on Cybersecurity 
Incidents and Digital Governance
16. Cybersecurity Incident
A cybersecurity incident is an event that threatens or affects the confidentiality, integrity or 
availability of information or systems.
Examples include:
● Data breaches
● Ransomware attacks
● Phishing attacks
● Unauthorized access
● Malware infections
● Website disruption
17. Example Case Study: Phishing Attack 
on an Organization
Consider a fictional company called ABC Retail.
Step 1: The Attack
An employee receives an email that appears to come from the company's IT department. 
The email asks the employee to urgently log into an account using a provided link.
Step 2: The Mistake
The employee clicks the link and enters their username and password.
Step 3: Unauthorized Access

The attacker obtains the login credentials and accesses the employee's account.
Step 4: Possible Impact
The attacker may:
● Read confidential information
● Access customer data
● Send phishing emails to other employees
Lesson
The organization should use:
● Employee awareness training
● Multi-Factor Authentication
● Email filtering
● Suspicious login detection
● Incident response procedures
18. Example Case Study: Ransomware 
Incident
Consider a fictional hospital called XYZ Hospital.
Step 1
An employee opens a malicious attachment.
Step 2
Ransomware enters the network and encrypts important files.
Step 3
The attackers demand payment.
Impact
● Patient information becomes inaccessible.

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
● Important services may be disrupted.
● The organization's operations are affected.
Lessons
Organizations need:
● Regular backups
● Employee cybersecurity training
● Security monitoring
● Updated systems
● Incident response and recovery plans
19. Digital Governance
Digital Governance refers to the policies, rules, responsibilities and processes used to manage 
digital technologies and information responsibly.
It helps organizations decide:
● Who is responsible for digital systems?
● How should data be managed?
● What security rules should be followed?
● How should privacy be protected?
● How should AI be used responsibly?
● What should happen when a cybersecurity incident occurs?
20. Importance of Digital Governance
Digital governance helps organizations:
● Protect information
● Define responsibilities
● Manage cybersecurity risks
● Protect privacy
● Ensure ethical technology use
● Respond effectively to incidents
● Build trust with users and customers

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Example
Suppose an organization has customer data. 
Good digital governance may define:
● Who can access the data
● Why they can access it
● How long the data should be stored
● What happens if a data breach occurs
● Who is responsible for responding
21. Relationship Between Cybersecurity, 
Ethics, AI and Governance
These concepts are connected.
Cybersecurity
Protects systems and information.
Privacy
Protects individuals' control over personal information.
Ethics
Helps determine whether technology is being used in an appropriate and fair manner.
Responsible AI
Ensures that AI is developed and used with appropriate safeguards.
Digital Governance
Provides the overall rules, responsibilities and processes for managing digital technologies.
Simple Way to Remember

SFIT SBIS Mr. Dhrupesh Savadia
Cybersecurity protects the system. 
Privacy protects personal information. 
Ethics guides what should be done.
Responsible AI guides how AI should be used.
Digital Governance provides the rules and responsibilities.
22. Important Differences
Information Security vs Cybersecurity
Information Security is the broader concept of protecting information in any form.
Cybersecurity mainly focuses on protecting digital systems, networks, devices and digital 
information from cyber threats.
Example
Protecting a physical confidential document in a locked cupboard is part of Information 
Security.
Protecting an online database from hackers is part of Cybersecurity.
Threat vs Attack
Threat: A potential danger.
Attack: An actual attempt to exploit a weakness.
Example
A known software vulnerability is a potential threat.
A hacker actually exploiting that vulnerability is an attack.
Privacy vs Security

23. Chapter Summary
This chapter explains that modern organizations depend heavily on information systems and 
therefore must protect their data and digital infrastructure.
The major objectives of information security are explained through the CIA Triad:
● Confidentiality – preventing unauthorized access
● Integrity – ensuring information remains accurate and unaltered
● Availability – ensuring systems and information are available when required 
Organizations face many security threats, including:
● Malware
● Phishing
● Social engineering
● Password attacks
● Denial-of-Service attacks
● Insider threats
To reduce these risks, organizations use security controls, including:
● Preventive controls
● Detective controls
● Corrective controls
Modern information systems also create important privacy and ethical issues, especially 
regarding the collection and use of personal data.
With the increasing use of Artificial Intelligence, organizations must focus on AI Ethics and
Responsible AI. Important principles include:
● Fairness
● Transparency
● Accountability
● Privacy
● Safety
● Human oversight

12. Responsible AI means developing and using AI safely, fairly and responsibly.
13. Digital Governance provides rules and responsibilities for managing digital
